title: Master Theorem
summary: Direct method to solve recurrences divide and conquer of the form T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n). Includes applicability conditions, parameter extraction, calculation of the critical exponent, cases 1, 2 and 3, regularity condition, solved examples and cases where the theorem does not apply.

learningObjectives.text: Recognize when a recurrence has the canonical form T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n).
Correctly extract the parameters a, b and f(n) from a divide and conquer recurrence.
Calculate the critical exponent p=log_b(a) and use n^p as a comparison boundary.
Apply case 1 when f(n) grows polynomially slower than n^p.
Apply case 2 when f(n) grows at the same rate as n^p.
Apply case 3 when f(n) grows polynomially faster than n^p and meets regularity.
Verify the regularity condition a·f(n/b) ≤ c·f(n), with 0<c<1, when trying to apply case 3.
Detect recurrences where the Master Theorem does not apply, even if the recurrence appears close to the canonical form.
Distinguish that the Master Theorem gives only a bound Θ, not the complete efficiency function.

terms.label: Master Theorem
terms.definition: Method to directly solve certain recurrences divide and conquer of the form T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n).

terms.label: to
terms.definition: Number of recursive subproblems generated by each call.

terms.label: b
terms.definition: Factor by which the size of each subproblem is reduced. At T(n/b), b must be greater than 1.

terms.label: f(n)
terms.definition: Non-recursive cost of splitting, combining, or doing local work in a call.

terms.label: critical exponent
terms.definition: Value p=log_b(a). Deendes the boundary n^p against which f(n) is compared.

terms.label: Border n^p
terms.definition: Function n^(log_b a) that separates the three cases of the Master Theorem.

terms.label: ε
terms.definition: Positive constant used to require polynomial separation between f(n) and n^p. There must exist some ε>0.

terms.label: Polynomial separation
terms.definition: Growth difference strong enough for f(n) to be below n^(p-ε) or above n^(p+ε).

terms.label: Regularity condition
terms.definition: Required condition in case 3: a·f(n/b) ≤ c·f(n), for some constant c with 0<c<1 and n sufficiently large.

terms.label: Mutually exclusive cases
terms.definition: Property of the three cases of the Master Theorem: if one applies correctly, the others do not apply.

blocks.title: Applicability decision and case

learningObjectives.text: Solve the base examples using the complete procedure.

explanation.text: We identify the components of recurrence: two subproblems (a=2), halving (b=2) and linear combination cost (f(n)=cn).
We calculate the critical exponent p using the logarithm of a to base b. This gives us the boundary function n^1.
We compare the external cost f(n) with the frontier n^p. In this case, both grow at the same rate (linear).
Since f(n) is of the same order as n^p, we apply case 2 of the Master Theorem.
The endal result adds a logarithmic factor to the boundary function, resulting in a complexity of n log n.
We extract the parameters: there are 4 subcalls, each reduces the size by half, and the external cost is linear.
The critical exponent p=2 deendes a quadratic boundary n^2.
We compare f(n)=n with n^2. Since n is polynomially smaller than n^2, we look for an epsilon that demonstrates this separation.
We verify that n indeed grows slower than n^(2-1)=n^1.
Since f(n) is polynomially smaller than the boundary, we apply Case 1.
The total complexity is dominated by the work on the leaves, which is of quadratic order.
We identify a=4, b=2 and a cubic external cost f(n)=n^3.
The boundary is still n^2, but now f(n) is n^3.
We observe that n^3 grows polynomially faster than n^2. We use epsilon=1 to validate it.

explanation.text: It seems to be Case 3, but this necessarily requires verifying the regularity condition.
We evaluate the regularity condition: the cost of the subproblems must be a fraction of the original cost.
We endd c=1/2, which must be less than 1. The regularity is satisfied.
By dominating the work at the root (external cost), the endal complexity is the order of f(n), that is, cubic.
